title: Fixing Bad Status Design
intro: Most UX effort goes into the moment of action. But **post-action UX** — what happens after users click Submit — is where confusion actually lives, especially in enterprise.

learn.title: The post-action gap
learn.text:
Enterprise workflows span people, approvals, dependencies, and backend processes. Users can handle complexity — but they struggle when the system's **actual state is unclear**.

The real usability burden shifts to what happens AFTER the action. Yet most teams spend all their design effort on the action itself.

**Status is a time-based problem, not a single-screen one.** It's about communicating state over the life of a workflow — not just at the moment of submission.

The principle behind this: NN/g's **visibility of system status** heuristic. Users need to know what's happening, what happened, and what's next.

right.label: Where users struggle
items: Do I need to do anything?
Is it stuck or just slow?

try.q: Why is status design especially hard in enterprise software?
options: Workflows span people, approvals, and async processes — state is distributed
Enterprise companies have smaller design teams
try.explain: Enterprise workflows involve multiple people, approvals, and backend processes. The system's state is distributed across all of them.

learn.title: Common status design failures
learn.text:
**Vague labels:** "Submitted" or "In Progress" says nothing useful. "Pending" could mean review, sync, another team's work, a nightly job, or a broken state.

**Disappearing toasts:** "Saved" or "Submitted" flashes briefly — easy to miss, doesn't say where the item went or who has it.

**Generic spinners:** Fine for short waits. For longer or unpredictable waits, they give no sense of duration or what's happening.

**Dashboard of badges:** Moving confusion to another screen. Tables of timestamps and badges can't show which items are healthy, stuck, or waiting.

**Silent table updates:** Something changed in the table — but what? When?

**Hidden costs:** Users resubmit, refresh, check email, ask coworkers, and build side spreadsheets. Unreliable status erodes product trust.

try.q: Why is "Pending" a bad status label?
options: It could mean at least 5 different things — review, sync, queue, error, or someone else's action
try.explain: "Pending" is ambiguous — it hides the actual system state. Users can't tell if something is in review, queued, waiting on someone, or broken.

learn.title: What good status design looks like
learn.text:
**Pair the state with its meaning:**
"Submitted for manager review" instead of "Submitted." Say what the status means for the user's work.

**State ownership and next steps:**
Say who holds the next step and what the system is waiting on. "Waiting for finance approval — expected by tomorrow."

**Signal when no action is needed:**
Explicitly tell users when they can leave: "No action needed. Expected completion by tomorrow morning."

**Keep status visible over time:**
Use persistent locations, timestamps, and status history — not disappearing messages. "Changes saved at 2:14 PM" stays visible.

**Show what changed:**
Updates should say what changed, when, and what happens next.

**Design post-action states as part of the core workflow** — not as an afterthought bolted on with badges and filters.

try.q: What makes "Submitted for manager review" better than "Submitted"?
options: It tells the user who has it and what's happening next
It uses more words, which feels more professional
try.explain: The improved version tells users the state (submitted), who has it (manager), and what's happening (review). No ambiguity.

test.q: What NN/g heuristic does the article use to frame status design?
test.explain: The article frames status as a visibility problem — users need to see what's happening, what happened, and what's next.

test.q: Why are disappearing toast notifications problematic for status communication?
options: They're easy to miss and don't say where the item went or who has it
They cause performance issues on mobile
They only work on desktop browsers
test.explain: Toasts flash briefly — easy to miss, and they carry no information about what happens next or who owns the next step.

test.q: What do users resort to when status design is unreliable?
options: Resubmitting, refreshing, asking coworkers, and building side spreadsheets
test.explain: Bad status design forces workarounds: resubmitting requests, refreshing pages, asking colleagues, and tracking in spreadsheets.

test.q: What information should a good status message include?
options: What state it's in, who owns the next step, and whether user action is needed
A link to the support page
test.explain: Good status = state + ownership + next steps + whether the user needs to act. Anything less creates ambiguity.

test.q: The article argues status indicators should be designed as:
options: Part of the core workflow — not bolted on as an afterthought
Email notifications instead of in-app indicators
test.explain: Post-action states are part of the workflow, not an add-on. Bolted-on badges and filters just move confusion to another screen.
